You are a Principal Systems Architect and Lead Cybersecurity Engineer specializing in software supply chain security, cross-platform systems programming, and cloud infrastructure.

We are designing and planning a comprehensive software supply chain security tool called "WhoaThere". The core goal of WhoaThere is to limit the blast radius of, or completely prevent, malicious npm and pip package attacks (such as dependency confusion, typo-squatting, malicious postinstall scripts, and data exfiltration).

The solution must consist of two tiers:

  1. WhoaThere CLI (Local Engine): A cross-platform developer tool running on macOS (Intel/M-series), Windows, Linux, and inside Docker containers. It must intercept package installs and isolate untrusted setup/install scripts.
  2. WhoaThere Vault (VPC Proxy): A secure, high-performance, caching upstream proxy deployed within a hardened VPC. It acts as a private registry mirror that pulls, detonates/scans, and caches public packages to speed up builds and block malicious updates.

Please provide a highly detailed, production-grade technical design document covering the following sections:

1. System & Language Selection Architecture

  • Recommend the best language (e.g., Rust vs. Go) to build the CLI and Proxy, weighing cross-platform compiling (macOS/Win/Linux), binary footprint, and memory safety.
  • Explain the interception mechanism: how exactly will the CLI intercept 'npm install' or 'pip install' workflows natively without breaking standard developer tooling (e.g., wrapper scripts, aliases, or customized configurations)?

2. Cross-Platform Local Isolation Strategy

Because we need to support macOS, Windows, and Linux locally, we cannot rely solely on Linux cgroups or namespaces. Detail a viable, unified strategy for isolating malicious install scripts (like npm's 'postinstall' or pip's 'setup.py' execution) across:

  • Linux & Docker Containers (e.g., seccomp, namespaces)
  • macOS (handling Apple Silicon security and sandbox limitations)
  • Windows (handling cmd/powershell execution and file system access)
  • Consider if a lightweight WebAssembly (WASM) runtime, virtualization, or OS-native sandboxing APIs is the right path here.

3. VPC Proxy & Caching Architecture

Provide an architectural breakdown of the "WhoaThere Vault" proxy deployed inside an AWS or general cloud VPC:

  • Network topology: Subnet layouts, NAT/Internet Gateway positioning, and how it completely isolates downstream resources from the public internet.
  • The Detonation Pipeline: The lifecycle of a cache-miss. When a new package is requested, how does the proxy fetch it, dynamically scan/detonate it, verify hashes, and safely append it to the cache?
  • Performance & Caching: How to optimize the storage layer for ultra-low latency package delivery to hundreds of developer machines and CI/CD runners simultaneously.

4. Step-by-Step Phased Engineering Roadmap

  • Phase 1: MVP Local CLI (Which OS and ecosystem to target first, minimal isolation).
  • Phase 2: Advanced Cross-Platform Isolation (Hardening macOS/Windows/Linux sandboxing).

Research Memo: WhoaThere Vault Greenfield Plan

Docs checked June 25, 2026. No files edited.

Working Thesis

Build the core Vault as an AWS-hosted, VPC-native service first, with Cloudflare as an optional edge/Zero Trust layer rather than the system of record. AWS has the cleaner primitives for private package consumption: PrivateLink lets consumer VPCs reach the service without internet gateways, NAT, public IPs, VPN, or Direct Connect, and traffic stays on the AWS network. (docs.aws.amazon.com) (docs.aws.amazon.com) Cloudflare is attractive for global cache distribution, Zero Trust policy, R2 storage economics, and Workers orchestration, but Workers VPC is still marked beta in current docs. (developers.cloudflare.com)

AWS vs Cloudflare Deployment Tradeoffs

AWS-first: Use NLB + PrivateLink endpoint service for customer VPC ingress; ECS/Fargate, EKS, Batch, or isolated EC2 workers for proxy, scanner, and detonation; S3 for immutable blobs; DynamoDB/RDS for package metadata and verdicts; SQS/EventBridge/Step Functions for miss workflows. Step Functions is a good fit for auditable, multi-step workflows and integrates with ECS/Fargate, EKS, SQS, Lambda, and Batch. (docs.aws.amazon.com)

Pros: best private VPC story, mature subnet routing controls, controlled egress via NAT/Network Firewall, strong IAM/KMS/VPC endpoint model, good fit for customer CI in AWS. Cons: multi-region latency/replication planning, NAT/firewall cost, more infrastructure ownership, less globally distributed by default.

Cloudflare-first: Use Workers as package registry façade, R2 for blob storage, Workers Cache for hot objects, Queues/Workflows for miss orchestration, Containers for heavier scan/detonation workloads. R2 is designed for large unstructured object storage without typical egress bandwidth fees. (developers.cloudflare.com) Queues support guaranteed delivery, batching, retries, delays, and dead-letter queues. (developers.cloudflare.com) Workflows support durable multi-step execution with retries and persisted state. (developers.cloudflare.com) Containers can run full Linux-like runtimes and resource-intensive code. (developers.cloudflare.com)

Pros: global low-latency serving, simpler edge auth/rate limiting, strong distribution economics. Cons: package detonation wants hard sandboxing and private network controls; Workers Cache is per data center rather than globally replicated by Cache API writes. (developers.cloudflare.com) Workers VPC/private routing is promising but beta, so it is risky as the only private connectivity foundation. (developers.cloudflare.com)

AWS CodeArtifact should be treated as a baseline/buy comparison, not the target architecture. It already supports npm and pip, upstream public repositories, and on-demand fetch/store from public registries. (docs.aws.amazon.com) (docs.aws.amazon.com) The open question is whether it can be wrapped without allowing unscanned packages to become reachable before Vault policy approval.

Network Topology

Recommended topology has three planes:

Serving plane: Developer/CI private subnet -> customer interface VPC endpoint -> Vault PrivateLink endpoint service -> NLB -> registry proxy. Consumer VPC route tables/security groups deny direct public registry egress. Use private hosted zones so registry.company or scoped npm/pip config resolves privately.

Miss/fetch plane: Only miss fetchers have controlled internet egress. They sit in egress subnets routed through AWS Network Firewall and NAT. NAT allows private subnet instances to initiate outbound connections while preventing unsolicited inbound connections. (docs.aws.amazon.com) Network Firewall supports stateful filtering, domain/IP controls, and Suricata-compatible inspection. (docs.aws.amazon.com) Allow only npm/PyPI/public metadata endpoints plus required OS mirrors if detonation needs them.

Detonation plane: Run package installs/builds in isolated, ephemeral workers with no route to internal services, no reusable credentials, blocked IMDS, tight CPU/memory/time limits, fresh filesystem, and captured process/file/network telemetry. Consider two modes: offline detonation for static/install behavior, and instrumented egress through a recording proxy for packages that expect network access. Never let detonation containers share the serving plane network.

Cloudflare/private option: Cloudflare One can connect private networks via Tunnel, Mesh, or WAN; Tunnel is outbound-only from the private network, while Mesh/WAN can support broader site connectivity. (developers.cloudflare.com) Workers VPC can connect Workers to private APIs/services in AWS or elsewhere, but plan around beta risk. (developers.cloudflare.com)

Cache-Miss Detonation Lifecycle

  1. Resolver receives npm packument/simple API request or tarball/wheel URL. npm clients can use compatible registries, scoped registries, and .npmrc; lockfiles carry resolved and integrity fields that affect mirror behavior. (docs.npmjs.com) (docs.npmjs.com) pip expects the Python Simple Repository API, including normalized names, project detail pages, file links, and recommended hashes. (packaging.python.org)
  1. On miss, fetch metadata and candidate artifact into quarantine CAS. Compute SHA-256/SHA-512, store origin URL, headers, time, package manager metadata, yanked/deprecated state, and upstream integrity.
  1. Enqueue scan workflow: static manifest scan, known vulnerability/malware checks, maintainer/provenance signals, install/build script detection, native binary detection, dependency expansion.
  1. Detonate selected artifacts in sandbox matrix: npm install with lifecycle scripts enabled; pip wheel install; sdist build where relevant; OS/arch variants only where policy needs them.
  1. Verdict: allow, deny, manual_review, expired_revalidate. Only allow promotes blob and generated metadata into the serving namespace.
  1. Serve behavior on first miss must be designed deliberately. Package managers do not handle arbitrary async admission well. The planning effort should compare blocking install until verdict, returning a deterministic policy failure with a prewarm command, and lockfile-based pre-admission for CI.

Content-Addressed Storage

Use immutable object keys by digest, not origin URL: blobs/sha256/ab/<digest>. Store ecosystem aliases separately: npm name@version -> digest + integrity + dist-tags snapshot; PyPI normalized project/file -> digest + hash fragment + wheel tags + requires-python + yanked status.

Generate served metadata from Vault state, not directly from upstream. For npm, rewrite tarball URLs to Vault and preserve integrity. For pip, emit Simple API HTML/JSON with hash fragments and normalized names. Keep upstream metadata snapshots versioned because dist-tags, yanks, deprecations, and package metadata can change while blobs remain immutable.

S3 object metadata can hold small fixed fields, but user metadata is limited and awkward to mutate after upload, so verdicts and rich provenance should live in DB tables, not only object metadata. (docs.aws.amazon.com)

Performance Bottlenecks

Cold misses are dominated by upstream fetch latency, artifact size, scan queue depth, and detonation runtime. Warm hits should be bounded by metadata lookup plus object streaming.

Hot paths to benchmark: metadata fanout for npm dependency trees; pip resolver behavior across many project pages and wheels; large tarball/wheel streaming; PrivateLink/NLB throughput per AZ; scanner CPU; dynamic sandbox startup; NAT/firewall egress bottlenecks; Cloudflare Cache hit ratio if used. Cloudflare Cache API writes are local to the originating data center, so do not assume a single cache fill makes a global hot cache. (developers.cloudflare.com)

Experiments and Open Questions

Measure protocol compatibility across npm, yarn, pnpm, pip, Poetry, and uv.

Prototype first-miss UX: blocking install vs prewarm/admission API vs lockfile submission.

Determine minimum useful detonation matrix for npm scripts, Python wheels, and Python sdists.

Benchmark CAS serving with 1,000 concurrent CI jobs and realistic npm/pip dependency graphs.

Validate egress controls: prove CI cannot bypass Vault to reach npmjs/PyPI.

Test metadata correctness for npm dist-tags, lockfile registry switching, PyPI yanked files, hash fragments, and Requires-Python.

Compare AWS-only, Cloudflare-only, and hybrid latency/cost for warm and cold installs.

Decide whether CodeArtifact can be reused as upstream cache without violating “scan before serve.”

Research Memo: Endpoint CLI Interception And Isolation

Working Hypothesis For first macOS/Linux endpoints, WhoaThere should start with a transparent CLI launcher plus OS-level process isolation, not a package-manager fork. The launcher preserves developer workflows, captures intent, resolves package/script risk, then runs the real tool under a constrained environment. Endpoint-level observation should be a backstop for missed invocations such as absolute paths or python -m pip.

npm / pip Interception Options

Best first layer. Preserve argv/stdin/stdout/exit code, call the real binary, and attach policy metadata to the process tree. This should not rewrite user commands except for explicit, visible policy modes.

  1. PATH shims for npm, npx, pip, pip3

npm supports config through npm_config_* environment variables and .npmrc; pip supports command-line options, env vars, and config files with defined precedence. Use this to point at a registry/index policy proxy, set cache locations, or request reports without changing project files. Risk: command-line flags override env/config, so this is not enforcement by itself.

  1. Config/environment steering

npm has lifecycle scripts for install, postinstall, prepare, etc.; npm v11 also exposes script approval controls such as allow-scripts and strict-allow-scripts. pip can produce an install JSON report with --dry-run --report, useful for dependency intent before installing. For npm, avoid silently forcing --ignore-scripts; it changes semantics and will break packages. For pip, remember that build isolation is not a security sandbox; source builds still run package-controlled build backend code.

  1. Resolution-before-execution

Linux: eBPF/audit/fanotify/LSM-style observation can catch absolute-path invocations and child process behavior. macOS: Endpoint Security is the supported observation/control plane for process/file events, but it is not a general-purpose sandbox. Use it to correlate and block obvious escapes, not as the only containment boundary.

  1. Endpoint backstop

LD_PRELOAD / DYLD_* interposition is brittle, shell-specific, SIP-sensitive on macOS, and easy to bypass. TLS MITM also risks breaking private registries and developer auth flows.

  1. Avoid as primary strategy

Script Isolation Strategy Linux should be the stronger initial enforcement target. Use a rootless sandbox around the install process: user/mount/network/PID namespaces, read-only host binds, writable project/cache/tmp binds, seccomp for syscall reduction, cgroups for resource caps, and Landlock where available for extra filesystem and TCP restrictions. Landlock is useful because unprivileged processes can restrict themselves, but availability and ABI differ by kernel.

For npm, the practical first mode is “sandbox the whole install,” because npm lifecycle scripts execute as part of the install flow. A stronger later mode is two-phase: install with scripts suppressed, then replay approved lifecycle scripts in per-package sandboxes while matching npm’s environment/order closely enough to avoid breakage.

For pip, prefer “resolve/download/build/install” separation: use pip install --dry-run --report to identify artifacts, prefer wheels, build sdists in a sandboxed build area with constrained network, then install produced wheels into the target venv. Python venv helps avoid system pollution but is not a security boundary.

macOS has weaker native CLI isolation. App Sandbox is entitlement/app-oriented, not a drop-in sandbox for arbitrary developer commands. Product options are: run the whole install inside a lightweight VM, use Endpoint Security plus restrictive process/user/network policy as partial containment, or prototype private Seatbelt profiles only as a research spike, not as a dependable product foundation.

Limitations WASM is not a general answer for npm/pip install scripts. It sandboxes modules well, but arbitrary package installs expect POSIX shells, compilers, native modules, Python/Node runtimes, filesystem layout, network, and platform-specific tooling.

Virtualization gives the cleanest macOS containment, but can break native host installs: paths, symlinks, filesystem events, permissions, native artifacts, performance, and “install into my real project” expectations all need testing.

OS-native sandboxing is asymmetric. Linux has composable primitives; macOS has good telemetry/control APIs but no supported, ergonomic equivalent to Linux namespaces/seccomp/Landlock for arbitrary CLI tools.

Planning Experiments Measure breakage on real projects: npm install, npm ci, npx, npm exec, pip install -r, python -m pip, venv installs, private registries, editable installs, git dependencies.

Test hostile packages against policies: read ~/.ssh, npm/PyPI tokens, env vars, cloud creds; write outside project; spawn shells; network exfiltrate; persist via shell profiles or launch agents.

Build a compatibility matrix for packages with install/build behavior: esbuild, sharp, playwright, node-gyp packages, cryptography, numpy/scipy, torch, local sdists, editable Python projects.

Decide policy UX: block, prompt, approve-list, team policy file, registry-only allow, offline build, and global install behavior.

Prototype macOS containment paths head-to-head: Endpoint Security-only, lightweight VM, and unsupported sandbox profile spike. The planning effort should choose based on breakage rate and security delta, not elegance.

Sources: npm scripts, npm install config, npm config env, pip install, pip configuration, Python venv, Linux Landlock, Linux seccomp, Linux namespaces, Apple Endpoint Security, WebAssembly security, Wasmtime security.

Threat-Model Memo: WhoaThere Plan-To-Build-A-Plan

Scope WhoaThere intercepts local npm/pip installs and routes package resolution/download through a VPC proxy mirror with scanning and detonation. The design must assume attackers know the tool exists and will optimize for bypass, delayed activation, and environment-aware behavior.

Primary Bypass And Evasion Risks

| Risk | Likely attacker technique | Required mitigation direction | Acceptance test before design lock | |---|---|---|---| | Install script abuse | preinstall, postinstall, setup.py, PEP 517 build hooks, npm lifecycle scripts executing shell, curl, node, python, or native tools | Default-deny or policy-gate install-time execution; sandbox build hooks; capture process tree, filesystem writes, network attempts, env reads | Malicious package tries install-script reverse shell, credential read, and curl exfil. Install is blocked or fully contained with auditable evidence | | Runtime-loaded payloads | Benign package at install, malicious code fetched or decrypted on first import/run | Static + dynamic scanning must include import-time and representative runtime detonation, not only install-time | Package passes install but downloads payload on import / require; system detects or blocks network/runtime behavior | | DNS and exfiltration | DNS TXT lookups, HTTPS to attacker infra, package-manager telemetry abuse, encoded data in URLs | Egress policy during detonation and optionally during install; DNS logging and deny rules; classify unusual destinations | Package attempts DNS and HTTPS exfil of env vars; detector records attempted domain, payload shape, and blocks | | Maintainer account takeover | Legit package publishes malicious patch/minor version under trusted name | Trust cannot be based only on package identity; require provenance, version-diff risk scoring, maintainer-change alerts, publish anomaly detection | Previously trusted package publishes version with new lifecycle script and obfuscated code; release is quarantined pending review | | Dependency confusion | Internal package name resolved from public registry; higher public semver wins | Namespace policy, registry pinning, private-package allowlist, lockfile enforcement, deny public fallback for internal scopes/names | Internal name exists privately and public attacker package has higher version; resolver must select private or fail closed | | Platform-specific packages | Payload hidden in optional deps, OS/CPU-specific wheels, npm os/cpu, conditional exports | Detonate across target platform matrix; inspect all artifacts, not only current developer platform | Package is benign on macOS but malicious on Linux CI; Linux artifact is scanned and flagged before approval | | Native extensions | Malicious .node, .so, .dylib, .pyd, Rust/Go/C++ build scripts, binary wheels | Binary analysis, build sandboxing, syscall/network tracing, signed/provenance-aware binary policy | Native extension tries filesystem credential scrape or network call during build/import; blocked or reported | | Lockfile and package-manager edge cases | Alternate package managers, lockfile overrides, git/tarball/file deps, npm aliasing, pip direct URLs, extras, hashes bypassed | Full parser support for npm, pnpm, yarn, pip, poetry, uv; reject unsupported dependency spec types by policy | Test matrix includes aliases, git deps, tarball URLs, local paths, extras, markers, overrides, workspace deps | | Delayed execution | Time bombs, environment checks, CI-only logic, hostname/user checks, sleep before payload | Detonation must simulate CI/dev/prod markers, accelerate sleeps, inspect suspicious guards, run multiple entrypoints | Package activates only when CI=true or after delay; analysis surfaces condition and payload |

Research Goals Required Before Design Lock

Validate whether WhoaThere can reliably intercept all relevant install paths: npm, npx, pnpm, yarn, pip, pipx, poetry, uv, build backends, Docker builds, CI runners, and direct registry API calls.

  1. Interception completeness

Define exactly what happens when the proxy mirror, scanner, detonator, or metadata service is unavailable. Security posture should default to block or require explicit break-glass approval.

  1. Fail-closed behavior

The proxy must resolve dependencies exactly like the native package manager, including lockfiles, markers, optional dependencies, peer dependencies, platform selectors, hashes, and registry precedence.

  1. Package-manager semantic fidelity

Decide which environments are simulated: developer laptop, Linux CI, production container, macOS, Windows, common Node/Python versions, and common env vars. Evasion resistance depends on this.

  1. Detonation realism

Clarify whether WhoaThere only protects install-time traffic or also runtime execution. If runtime is out of scope, say so explicitly and design compensating controls.

  1. Network-control boundary

I found no existing WhoaThere product notes in the repo, only the current WhoaThere Timer Swift app, so I’d structure this as a greenfield product decomposition memo.

Meta-Plan Shape

The meta-plan should produce a small set of parent goals, each with clear child-plan boundaries. Each goal should define:

  • Problem statement
  • In-scope / out-of-scope
  • Key decisions required
  • Research questions delegated to child plans
  • Deliverables
  • Acceptance criteria
  • Exit gate
  • Dependencies on other goals

The parent plan should avoid over-specifying implementation. Its job is to create well-bounded implementation-planning goals, not solve every subsystem now.

Recommended Workstreams

  1. Product Threat Model & MVP Scope
  • Define the first protected workflow: package install, build dependency fetch, container pull, artifact download, or CI dependency resolution.
  • Identify personas: developer laptop, build agent, security admin.
  • Deliverables: MVP use cases, abuse cases, non-goals, threat model, initial policy model.
  • Gate: one sharply defined “first workflow” with measurable protection value.
  1. Endpoint CLI / Local Agent
  • macOS/Linux CLI behavior, install/update model, auth, local config, logging, diagnostics.
  • Decide whether the endpoint is passive CLI, long-running daemon, shell wrapper, package-manager shim, network proxy client, or some mix.
  • Deliverables: CLI command map, local trust boundaries, endpoint lifecycle, UX flows.
  • Gate: user can install, authenticate, run a protected fetch/install flow, and inspect why something was allowed or blocked.
  1. VPC Proxy / Data Plane
  • Proxy placement, traffic routing, protocol support, TLS behavior, cache strategy, fail-open/fail-closed modes.
  • AWS and Cloudflare should be evaluated as deployment targets, but the parent plan should not prematurely commit unless deployment constraints are already known.
  • Deliverables: data-plane architecture options, latency budget, routing model, failure modes.
  • Gate: one selected deployment architecture for MVP with rollback and observability paths.
  1. Policy, Identity & Trust
  • Define policy subjects, resources, decisions, attestations, exceptions, and auditability.
  • Decide whether policies are local files, remote-managed, Git-backed, API-managed, or hybrid.
  • Deliverables: policy schema draft, identity model, enforcement semantics, exception workflow.
  • Gate: same policy decision can be explained consistently by CLI, proxy, and control plane.
  1. Control Plane & Admin Experience
  • Tenant/project model, API surface, dashboard/admin needs, policy distribution, audit log access.
  • Deliverables: control-plane domain model, API boundaries, admin workflows.
  • Gate: admin can define policy, see events, and understand enforcement outcomes.
  1. Detection Intelligence & Supply-Chain Signals
  • Vulnerability data, package reputation, provenance, lockfile diffing, SBOM, malicious package indicators, registry metadata.
  • Deliverables: signal inventory, source-of-truth decisions, freshness requirements, scoring/explanation model.
  • Gate: MVP can justify decisions using explicit, inspectable signals rather than opaque scoring.
  1. Security, Privacy & Compliance Baseline
  • Secrets handling, telemetry minimization, customer data boundaries, signing, updates, auditability.
  • Deliverables: security architecture review, privacy data map, key-management plan, secure update plan.
  • Gate: no MVP architecture depends on collecting unnecessary source code, secrets, or full network payloads.
  1. Operations, Deployment & Reliability
  • Deployment model for AWS/Cloudflare, observability, incident response, tenant isolation, SLOs.
  • Deliverables: environments, infra shape, logs/metrics/traces, backup/restore, runbooks.
  • Gate: MVP can be deployed, monitored, upgraded, and rolled back by engineering without heroics.

Phase Boundaries

Phase 0: Framing

  • Output: product thesis, first protected workflow, threat model, MVP non-goals.
  • Exit when the team agrees what WhoaThere blocks, warns on, records, and ignores.

Phase 1: Architecture Selection

  • Output: endpoint architecture, proxy architecture, policy model, deployment target recommendation.
  • Exit when major irreversible choices are documented with tradeoffs.

Phase 2: MVP Vertical Slice

  • Output: CLI + proxy + policy + audit path for one workflow.
  • Exit when a real developer flow can be protected end to end.

Phase 3: Alpha Hardening

  • Output: install/update, observability, admin workflow, failure modes, security review.
  • Exit when trusted internal users can run it without engineer supervision.

Phase 4: Beta / Design Partner Readiness

  • Output: multi-tenant controls, operational runbooks, clearer UX, integration docs.
  • Exit when external teams can onboard with bounded support.

Decision Gates

Use explicit gates between phases:

  • MVP workflow gate: Which workflow is protected first?
  • Endpoint gate: CLI-only, daemon, shim, local proxy, or hybrid?
  • Proxy gate: AWS-native, Cloudflare-native, or portable abstraction?
  • TLS/enforcement gate: observe-only, explicit proxy, transparent proxy, or package-manager integration?
  • Policy gate: local-first, remote-managed, GitOps, or hybrid?
  • Signal gate: which intelligence sources are authoritative for MVP?
  • Failure-mode gate: fail-open vs fail-closed by workflow and customer maturity.
  • Privacy gate: what data is never collected.

Acceptance Criteria For Parent Goals

Each parent goal should be accepted only when it produces child-plan-ready artifacts:

  • Clear owner and dependencies
  • Concrete user or operator workflow
  • Architectural decision records for major choices
  • Open questions separated into research tasks
  • MVP acceptance tests stated in product terms
  • Security/privacy implications called out
  • “Not now” list to prevent scope creep

Decide Now

These should be settled in the meta-plan:

  • First protected workflow
  • MVP user persona
  • Enforcement posture: block, warn, audit, or mixed
  • Initial endpoint OS: macOS, Linux, or both
  • Whether a VPC proxy is mandatory for MVP or part of a later deployment mode
  • Minimum policy semantics
  • Data collection boundaries
  • Fail-open/fail-closed defaults
  • Deployment target shortlist: AWS, Cloudflare, or dual-track spike

Research In Child Plans

These should not be over-decided in the parent plan:

  • Exact package-manager integrations
  • Transparent proxy mechanics
  • TLS interception vs metadata-only inspection
  • Registry-specific behavior
  • AWS vs Cloudflare implementation details
  • Cache design
  • SBOM/provenance formats
  • Vulnerability/reputation data providers
  • Signing/update mechanism details
  • Multi-tenant control-plane schema
  • Pricing/packaging assumptions

The strongest meta-plan would aim for one end-to-end MVP slice first: local endpoint captures a dependency-fetch workflow, sends it through a deployable proxy, evaluates a simple policy, records an audit event, and gives the developer an explainable allow/warn/block result.

I found no existing endpoint/interception/isolation goal-pack docs in ~/src/whoathere; current repo is a small macOS timer app. For a greenfield documentation artifact to be decision-complete, the goal pack should include this checklist:

Must-Have Checklist

  • Clear goal statement: what “endpoint”, “interception”, and “isolation” mean in WhoaThere terms, plus explicit non-goals.
  • Threat model: what risks are being controlled, such as package install scripts, dependency downloads, subprocesses, local network access, credential exfiltration, and DNS bypass.
  • Parallel implementation track:
  • macOS path: chosen interception mechanism, required privileges/entitlements, fallback limits, process attribution strategy, and how isolation applies to subprocess trees.
  • Linux path: chosen mechanism, such as network namespace plus firewall/proxy policy, privilege model, process attribution, and subprocess inheritance.
  • Shared behavior matrix showing what must behave identically across macOS and Linux.
  • npm workflow:
  • Covered commands: npm install, npm ci, npm run, lifecycle scripts, package manager subprocesses.
  • Endpoint allow/deny policy for registries, tarballs, git dependencies, postinstall downloads, telemetry, and lockfile drift.
  • Expected behavior for blocked endpoints and reproducibility requirements.
  • pip workflow:
  • Covered commands: pip install, pip download, editable installs, PEP 517 build isolation, VCS dependencies, wheels, source builds.
  • Endpoint policy for PyPI, package indexes, build backends, native toolchains, and post-install imports/scripts.
  • Required interfaces:
  • Policy file schema: endpoint rules, package-manager mode, platform overrides, default action, audit mode.
  • CLI contract: run command, inspect decision log, approve/deny endpoint, export report.
  • Interceptor contract: observed request shape, process identity, package context, decision result, failure reason.
  • Isolation contract: environment variables, DNS behavior, proxy/firewall behavior, subprocess inheritance, cleanup guarantees.
  • Event/log schema: timestamp, platform, process tree, command, package name/version when known, endpoint, rule matched, action.
  • Decision tables:
  • DNS vs direct IP behavior.
  • HTTPS CONNECT/proxy behavior.
  • localhost/private network handling.
  • Git SSH/HTTPS dependencies.
  • Cached/offline installs.
  • Native build tools invoking network calls.
  • Acceptance tests:
  • macOS and Linux tests for allowed registry access.
  • macOS and Linux tests for blocked unknown endpoint during npm install.
  • macOS and Linux tests for blocked unknown endpoint during pip install.
  • Lifecycle/postinstall script network attempt is captured and denied.
  • Subprocess network attempt inherits isolation.
  • DNS bypass/direct IP attempt is handled as specified.
  • Audit-only mode logs without blocking.
  • Report output matches documented schema.
  • Cleanup test proves no lingering firewall/proxy/network namespace state.
  • Operational requirements:
  • Minimum OS versions.
  • Required privileges.
  • Known unsupported cases.
  • Failure modes and user-facing remediation.
  • Security assumptions called out explicitly.

The biggest decision-completeness gaps to avoid are leaving the interception mechanism undecided per OS, omitting subprocess/package-manager lifecycle behavior, and failing to define the event/policy schemas before implementation.

The repo currently has no Vault/proxy/cloud goal-pack docs; README.md only covers the local timer app. For the goal pack to be decision-complete, it should include this checklist.

Must-Have Contents

  • README / index: goal, non-goals, target users, threat model summary, dependency map, and links to every ADR/test plan.
  • Deployment ADRs:
  • AWS-only ADR with chosen services, network boundary, secret custody, logging, cost, rollback, and operational burden.
  • Cloudflare-only ADR with Workers/Durable Objects/R2/KV/D1 choices, limits, secret custody, observability, rollback, and cost.
  • Hybrid ADR explaining why split control/data planes, trust boundaries, latency impact, failure modes, and which provider owns source of truth.
  • A final recommendation ADR with explicit decision criteria and rejection rationale for the other options.
  • Vault design:
  • Secret lifecycle: create, encrypt, rotate, revoke, expire, audit.
  • Access model: identity, tenancy, least privilege, break-glass, admin boundaries.
  • Key management: KMS/provider-specific custody, envelope encryption, rotation cadence, recovery limits.
  • Backup/restore and disaster recovery with RPO/RTO targets.
  • Proxy design:
  • Request flow diagrams for happy path, cache hit, cache miss, auth failure, upstream failure, and policy denial.
  • Authentication and authorization enforcement point.
  • Header/body handling rules, redaction, replay protection, request signing, rate limits.
  • Explicit “no secret leaves boundary except X” invariant.
  • Cache-miss detonation lifecycle:
  • Definition of cache miss and detonation trigger.
  • State machine: miss detected, lock/acquire, fetch/build, validate, publish, invalidate old entry, notify, retry/abort.
  • Concurrency behavior, duplicate suppression, idempotency key, poison-entry handling.
  • Blast-radius controls: per-tenant limits, circuit breakers, backoff, quarantine.
  • Audit trail for every detonation.
  • CAS/content-addressed storage:
  • Hash algorithm and canonicalization rules.
  • Object immutability, dedupe behavior, metadata schema, retention, GC.
  • Integrity verification on write/read, corruption handling, migration/versioning.
  • Relationship between CAS keys, cache keys, Vault records, and proxy responses.
  • Performance plan:
  • Latency budgets for p50/p95/p99 by path.
  • Cold start expectations, cache-hit ratio target, cache-miss detonation budget.
  • Throughput/rate-limit assumptions, payload size limits, provider quotas.
  • Load-test scenarios and capacity model for AWS, Cloudflare, and hybrid.
  • Fail-closed behavior:
  • Enumerated failure matrix: Vault unavailable, CAS unavailable, cache unavailable, provider auth failure, policy engine failure, partial deploy, stale config.
  • For each: user-visible result, HTTP status/error contract, retryability, alert, and audit event.
  • Explicit prohibition against falling back to permissive access, stale secrets, unsigned payloads, or unaudited bypasses.
  • Security/compliance:
  • Data classification, PII/secrets handling, log redaction, audit retention.
  • Supply-chain assumptions, deploy permissions, infrastructure change approval.
  • Incident response runbook and key compromise procedure.
  • Acceptance tests:
  • ADR completeness checks: every decision has alternatives, tradeoffs, owner, date, and revisit trigger.
  • End-to-end tests for cache hit, cache miss detonation, CAS integrity, Vault read/write, and proxy denial.
  • Negative tests proving fail-closed behavior.
  • Performance tests with stated pass/fail thresholds.
  • Deployment tests for AWS-only, Cloudflare-only, and hybrid paths, including rollback.
  • Security tests for unauthorized access, stale token, replay, tampered CAS object, and secret leakage in logs.

The biggest decision-completeness gap to avoid is documenting components without choosing ownership boundaries: the pack must say which system is authoritative for secrets, CAS objects, cache entries, policy, audit logs, and deployment state in each deployment model.

  • Four downstream phase goals that can be run next:

So the chain is:

current goal packs -> detailed architecture/planning artifacts -> downstream phase implementation plans -> working deployable system

Validation Already Present

Each goal pack has three built-in completion gates:

  • Required Deliverables: exact files/artifacts that must exist.
  • Acceptance Criteria: what must be true for the goal to count as handled.
  • Exit Gate: what must be satisfied before later planning or implementation can proceed.

The cross-goal validation is in:

  • interfaces-and-contracts.md, which ensures all required public/internal contracts are specified.
  • acceptance-test-matrix.md, which ensures the plans cover adversarial, compatibility, outage, performance, privacy, and audit scenarios.

Important Caveat

Right now, validation is documented and review-driven, not automated. A goal pack is “done” only when its deliverables exist, its acceptance criteria are met, its exit gate is satisfied, and it maps back to the interface/test matrices.

The strongest next improvement would be adding a global goal-pack-completion-checklist.md that requires traceability from every goal output to: deliverables, ADRs, interfaces, tests, owner, unresolved questions, and exit-gate signoff.

Reviewer Memo: GOAL-03 Endpoint Outputs

Scope reviewed: GOAL-03 objective, interfaces checklist, acceptance matrix. I did not edit files. No docs/whoathere/outputs/GOAL-03 artifacts exist yet, so this is a pre-review memo for those expected outputs.

Required Decisions

  • Interception: confirm PATH shims plus npm/pip config steering as the primary model; explicitly reject LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_*, package-manager forks, TLS MITM, and WASM as primary enforcement.
  • python -m pip: decide the real enforcement behavior, not just detection. Protected mode must either intercept it, block it, or document a fail-closed path.
  • npm steering: define CLI flag/config/env precedence, scoped registries, lockfile resolved host handling, integrity preservation, lifecycle visibility, workspaces, aliases, optional/peer deps, git/tarball/direct URL policy.
  • pip steering: define --index-url, config/env precedence, --dry-run --report limits, hash mode, Simple API behavior, sdists, wheels, editable installs, direct references, extras, markers, and private-index fallback.
  • Linux isolation: choose an enforceable backend with namespaces, seccomp, cgroups, Landlock where useful, filesystem mounts, network modes, and subprocess inheritance.
  • macOS isolation: do not overclaim native controls. Strong isolation should be VM-backed unless ADR-004 proves an enforceable alternative. Endpoint Security is telemetry/partial control, not a full sandbox.
  • Network policy: provide explicit decision tables for DNS, DoH, direct IP, HTTPS CONNECT, localhost, RFC1918, cloud metadata IPs, Git SSH, Git HTTPS, registries, telemetry, and build tools invoking network calls.
  • Cleanup: define normal, failure, timeout, crash, and signal cleanup guarantees for VMs, namespaces, helpers, mounts, proxies, firewall rules, sockets, temp dirs, and credentials.

Traps To Avoid

  • Treating registry/index steering as a security boundary. It is routing and compatibility glue; the sandbox/network layer must enforce.
  • Forgetting that command-line flags override config and env. Both npm and pip can bypass naive steering.
  • Assuming pip dry-run is side-effect-free. Metadata preparation and build backends can execute code depending on package form.
  • Letting npm run, lifecycle scripts, PEP 517 builds, native builds, git, curl, ssh, or spawned package managers escape the correlation/isolation boundary.
  • Allowing private registry fallback to public packages without explicit dependency-confusion policy.
  • Treating localhost/private networks as harmless. Local services, RFC1918 ranges, and metadata endpoints need deny/allow/record rules.
  • Leaving unsupported source types as prose warnings. CI and high-risk contexts must fail closed unless break-glass applies.

Validation Points

  • Native behavior: shims preserve argv, stdin/stdout/stderr, cwd, env redaction, signals, and exit code.
  • npm/pip compatibility maps to CT-001 through CT-009, especially npm ci, npx/npm exec, npm run, pip install -r --require-hashes, editable installs, direct URLs, and python -m pip.
  • Subprocess inheritance maps to CT-004 and CT-010 with process-tree correlation and inherited network/filesystem policy on macOS and Linux.
  • Network table is testable against DNS TXT/DoH, direct IP, localhost, RFC1918, Git SSH/HTTPS, registry access, and native build egress.
  • Cleanup maps directly to CT-011 and proves no lingering VM, namespace, proxy, firewall, mount, helper, socket, temp credential, or policy state after interrupted runs.
  • Completion record must show every GOAL-03 deliverable, ADR status, interface ownership, acceptance-test mapping, known gaps, and follow-up goals before marking complete.

Reviewer Memo: GOAL-04 Vault Outputs

Scope: future docs under ~/src/whoathere/docs/whoathere/outputs/GOAL-04, judged against GOAL-04, interfaces, and the acceptance matrix.

Required Decisions

  • ADR-005, ADR-006, ADR-007, and ADR-011 must each be real decisions, not cloud comparison prose. Include status, selected/rejected outcome, alternatives, security/ops/compat/cost impact, and revisit triggers.
  • AWS remains the default for hardened VPC/private-network detonation unless Cloudflare or hybrid clearly beats it across security, compatibility, cost, and operations.
  • Each AWS/Cloudflare/hybrid ADR must name the authoritative owner for secrets, KMS/envelope keys, CAS blobs, cache entries, metadata, verdicts, policy, audit logs, evidence bundles, deployment state, and rollback metadata.
  • The CodeArtifact baseline must answer the key question directly: can it prevent serving unscanned upstream packages before Vault approval? If not, reject or sharply constrain it.
  • The recommendation ADR must explain why rejected options are insufficient, not merely why the chosen one is convenient.

Traps To Avoid

  • Hybrid split-brain: do not put metadata in one provider, verdicts in another, and cache in both without one system of record and conflict resolution.
  • Treating Workers Cache, CDN cache, package-manager cache, or CodeArtifact upstream cache as authoritative approved content.
  • Serving upstream npm/PyPI metadata that still points clients at public tarball/file URLs.
  • Keying approval by package name/version only. Approval must bind to artifact digest plus ecosystem metadata context.
  • Rollback that restores config but accidentally reopens public-registry fallback or stale unapproved metadata.
  • Break-glass that becomes a broad allow rule. It must be scoped, time-bound, revocable, audited, and unavailable for unaudited bypasses.
  • “Fail open for developer convenience” leaking into CI, high-risk installs, scanner outage, ambiguous verdicts, or unsupported source types.

Validation Points

  • Scan-before-serve: prove every npm and PyPI path stores into quarantine first, validates integrity/hash, scans/detonates, writes verdict, then atomically promotes approved blob plus generated metadata.
  • CAS/storage: require separate quarantine/promoted namespaces, immutable digest keys, metadata snapshots, alias tables, retention/GC rules, tamper detection, and yanked/deprecated/dist-tag handling.
  • Cache-miss state machine: must include admission locks, duplicate suppression, idempotent retries, aborts, poison entries, circuit breakers, deterministic client responses, and audit events on every transition.
  • Fail-closed matrix: cover Vault, CAS, metadata DB, cache, provider auth, policy, scanner, detonator, stale config, partial deploy, and rollback. For each, require HTTP status/body, retryability, alert, audit event, break-glass applicability, and explicit no public fallback.
  • Secrets/key/DR: require secret lifecycle, KMS custody, envelope encryption, rotation, revocation, backup/restore, RPO/RTO, key compromise procedure, and evidence/audit retention.
  • Authority boundaries: authority-boundaries.md must match the ADRs exactly. Any mismatch is a blocking review finding.
  • 1000 concurrent CI warm-cache: performance-plan.md must define target latency/error SLO, warm metadata/artifact path, streaming behavior for large artifacts, cache/DB/object-store load model, benchmark fixture, and pass/fail thresholds for PT-001, PT-002, and PT-004.

Completion should be blocked until completion-record.md maps each GOAL-04 deliverable to acceptance evidence and names ownership for the relevant interface and test scenarios.

Top Finding No completed docs/whoathere/outputs/GOAL-05, GOAL-06, or GOAL-08 artifacts are present, so these cannot be accepted as completed outputs yet. The checked-in files are goal specifications. Completion requires the deliverables and completion-record.md files required by the execution objective and checklist.

GOAL-05: Policy, Identity, Audit The right acceptance bar is strict:

  • Policy must express subjects, resources, decisions, fail-closed defaults, internal namespace protection, lifecycle/build/import rules, network egress, source-type behavior, and developer-vs-CI posture.
  • Identity must cover tenant/project/user/machine/CI/service identities, signed policy provenance, offline behavior, and break-glass authority.
  • Audit must be append-only and emitted for allow, deny, quarantine, manual_review, and break_glass.
  • Audit events must reference evidence, not embed source, secrets, or full payloads.
  • Break-glass must never compile down to a durable allow rule. It needs identity, reason, scope, expiry, revocation, notification, and audit trail.

Validation points: same request gets explainable CLI and Vault decisions; outage policy can fail closed; break-glass expiry causes new decisions to fail closed; audit links actor, package digest, policy version, verdict, reason, evidence reference, and correlation ID.

Refs: GOAL-05 deliverables, GOAL-05 acceptance

GOAL-06: Detection And Detonation The core invariant is scan-before-serve: nothing becomes warm-cache content until an allow verdict exists.

Required decisions to preserve:

  • Fetch untrusted artifacts into quarantine CAS first.
  • Hash and preserve upstream integrity before scanning.
  • Static, provenance, reputation, anomaly, and detonation signals feed an explainable verdict.
  • Promotion is only from quarantine to serving namespace after approval.
  • Detonation matrix must include npm lifecycle scripts, npm import/require, Python wheel install/import, Python sdist/PEP 517, Linux CI with CI=true, macOS developer context, native extensions, no-network, and recorded-egress modes.
  • Evidence model must cover process tree, filesystem writes, network/DNS attempts, import-time behavior, suspicious guards/delays, verdict reasons, and redaction state.

Traps to avoid: detonating only on the current developer OS, skipping Python import-time behavior, treating DNS as harmless metadata, allowing Git/tarball/direct URL bypasses, losing npm/pip resolver semantics, or promoting ambiguous/manual-review artifacts.

Refs: GOAL-06 lifecycle, GOAL-06 matrix

GOAL-08: Operations, Privacy, Reliability The operations plan must make privacy and failure behavior operational, not aspirational.

Must-hold decisions:

  • CI and high-risk installs fail closed on scanner, proxy, or policy outage.
  • Developer warning mode is only allowed when policy explicitly permits it.
  • Rollback cannot bypass scan-before-serve or serve unscanned packages.
  • Warm-cache SLO, cold-miss SLO, scanner backlog, and policy-service failure must be separately observable.
  • Incident response must include malicious package quarantine, false-positive rollback/remediation, outage handling, policy misconfiguration, and customer notification.
  • Default telemetry must exclude source code, secrets/tokens, full environment dumps, full network payloads, and complete filesystem contents.

Validation points: redaction tests for malicious log output; data inventory/export/delete behavior; secure update signing/notarization/checksum verification; backup/restore for metadata, policy, audit logs, and object storage; incident drills for malicious package, false positive, Vault outage, and policy outage.

Refs: GOAL-08 privacy, GOAL-08 reliability

Cross-Cutting Rejection Criteria Reject outputs if they:

  • Allow permissive fallback during CI, high-risk installs, unsupported source types, or scanner/proxy/policy outage.
  • Store raw source, secrets, full env dumps, full filesystem snapshots, or full network payloads as routine evidence.
  • Let break-glass outlive its approval window or avoid audit.
  • Treat evidence as prose instead of a structured, referenceable model.
  • Leave acceptance tests unmapped, especially AT-001 through AT-010, OT-001 through OT-008, and PA-001 through PA-003.
  • Declare completion without required deliverables, interface ownership, test traceability, ADR status, and completion records.

Primary validation matrix: acceptance-test-matrix.md

Core Recommendation Make Phase 4 a profile-gated detection system, not a generic scanner. The docs already require promotion only after an artifact-class evidence profile passes (GOAL-06, Phase 4), but the actual minimum allow profiles are still TBD (contract). Treat those profiles as the first implementation deliverable.

Evidence Profiles Create versioned profiles before worker implementation:

  • npm.registry_tarball.v1: manifest/lifecycle static scan, SRI/hash verification, maintainer/release diff, Linux CI lifecycle detonation, require/import smoke, no-network plus recorded-egress modes.
  • npm.native_extension.v1: all registry tarball evidence plus native build/import on Linux and selective macOS VM when policy/platform requires it.
  • npm.untrusted_source.v1: git/tarball/direct URL defaults to manual_review or deny; no CI auto-allow without pinned digest/ref/source policy.
  • pypi.wheel.v1: metadata/hash/yanked/tag validation, wheel tag platform coverage, install/import smoke, native marker handling.
  • pypi.sdist_pep517.v1: isolated PEP 517 build, build dependencies through Vault, generated wheel install/import smoke.
  • pypi.editable_vcs_direct.v1: manual_review or deny by default.

Each profile should declare mandatory jobs, optional jobs, platform target set, source types never auto-allowable, timeout behavior, and whether human review can approve after evidence is complete. Missing mandatory evidence must return pending, manual_review, deny, or 503, never allow (hard rules).

Scanner/Detonator Schema Extend the planned job contract (schema) with implementation fields:

  • profile_id, profile_version, job_kind, job_action_set
  • worker_image_digest, toolchain_versions, sandbox_backend
  • environment_profile: CI=true, hostname/user variants, sleep policy
  • network_mode: none, recorded_egress, blocked
  • expected_evidence_refs, reason_codes, resource_usage
  • idempotency_key: admission + digest + profile + platform + action hash

Keep the terminal states as planned, but enforce one aggregation rule: only all mandatory passed jobs can contribute to allow (line 121).

Fixtures Build fixtures around GOAL-09 ownership, not a blanket “Phase 4 owns all ATs” model. Phase 4 should primarily own AT-004, AT-005, AT-008, AT-009, OT-002, OT-003, and contribute detection evidence to AT-001/002/003/006/007 (Phase 4 test scope).

Fixture requirements:

  • Include expected evidence assertions, not just expected verdicts.
  • Use local listeners/blackholed domains and fake canary secrets.
  • Add benign-control versions for maintainer-takeover and version-diff tests.
  • For each fixture, assert process tree, fs events, DNS/network events, redaction outcome, and reason codes.

Manual Review Implement review as a digest/context-bound adjudication layer, not an override path. Approval should be possible only when integrity, source policy, redaction, and profile-mandatory jobs are complete. If mandatory evidence is missing, the only valid reviewer action is needs_more_evidence.

The review record should bind reviewer, rationale, digest, metadata context, source, policy version, evidence bundle, expiry, and resulting verdict candidate, matching the existing workflow (manual review).

Gates Recommended build gates:

  1. Schema gate: profile, job, evidence bundle, and review-decision schemas are versioned and contract-tested.
  2. Research gate: all six minimum allow profile rows are filled before any production cold-miss promotion for that class.
  3. Fixture gate: AT-001 through AT-009 pass with evidence assertions, not just verdict assertions.
  4. Outage gate: OT-002/OT-003 prove scanner failure, worker failure, timeout, and backlog never promote.
  5. Privacy gate: PA-001/PA-002 prove no secrets, source trees, full env dumps, or full payloads persist.
  6. Promotion gate: Phase 3 atomic promotion accepts only allow bound to CAS, metadata digest, policy version, evidence profile, and evidence bundle.

Net: start with profile registry + schemas, then static/provenance scanner, then Linux detonation workers, then evidence storage/review, then macOS selective workers. Do not enable profile promotion until its profile row and fixture gate are complete.

Findings

  • P0: deny decisions are only printed, not enforced. main always returns process status 0 after println!, while protect only renders exit_code=20 text. Before real execution, return a typed result and call std::process::exit(...); test denied/invalid policy paths never spawn. main.rs, lib.rs
  • P0: generated shims trust PATH and are shell-injection prone. Shims exec "whoathere" via shell, and shell_escape only escapes ", leaving $()/backticks live if a future absolute path contains shell syntax. Use canonical current_exe, robust single-quote escaping or native shims, and tests for PATH hijack, self-recursion, and $() paths. lib.rs, lib.rs, lib.rs
  • P1: policy loading is not in the wrapper path. policy check / check-source --policy load files, but protect ignores policy files and uses hardcoded default_decision. The safe wrapper should load policy before any child spawn, and unreadable/invalid/unknown-schema policy must deny. lib.rs, lib.rs, lib.rs
  • P1: policy/config schema versions are accepted blindly. schema_version is copied without compatibility checks in both policy and config parsers. Unknown versions should be hard errors for execution, with tests proving they fail closed. policy lib.rs, core lib.rs
  • P1: command classification is not enough to permit execution. npm ci and pip install -r ... can look protected from argv while source overrides live in .npmrc, pip config, lockfiles, requirements files, or env. Safe execution needs sanitized env/config plus Vault-only registry/index rewriting; add tests for direct URLs in lockfiles/requirements and ambient config. core lib.rs, core lib.rs
  • P1: AllowVaultOnly allows all loopback. If used for real package-manager execution, malware could call arbitrary local services on 127.0.0.1/::1. Restrict to an exact configured Vault origin/socket and test arbitrary loopback denial. sandbox lib.rs
  • P2: shim install can overwrite through existing paths/symlinks. std::fs::write(dest/name) follows symlinks and overwrites existing files. Use create_new, temp+rename, ownership/mode checks, and tests for pre-existing shim/symlink refusal. lib.rs

  • P1: Do not reuse AllowVaultOnly as the loopback contract. It currently allows vault.local, *.vault.local, 127.0.0.1, and ::1 (lib.rs). For this slice, add a distinct bind/egress check that accepts only parsed loopback IP socket addresses and rejects 0.0.0.0, ::, hostnames, and public/private LAN IPs.

Keep the first HTTP surface to control/introspection endpoints only.

Minimal SPI Put the SPI in whoathere-sandbox; keep whoathere-launch pure by accepting proofs only.

pub trait ProofProvider {
    fn provider_id(&self) -> ProofProviderId;
    fn prove_containment(&self, req: &ContainmentProofRequest) -> ContainmentProof;
    fn prove_vault_egress(&self, req: &VaultEgressProofRequest) -> EgressProof;
}

Required additions:

  • ProofProvenance: provider id/version, platform, mechanism (LinuxNamespace, MacosVmBeta, LinuxNftables, MacosPf, TestOnly), isolation/session id, redacted evidence refs.
  • ProofSubject: launch/session id plus optional runtime dir/workspace identity. Containment and egress proofs must match the same subject.
  • EgressPolicyScope: require DefaultDenyExceptConfiguredVault, not just sample destination checks.
  • Make verified proof fields/constructors private or provider-minted. Leave missing() and operator_asserted() public.
  • Add UnavailableProofProvider as the default local provider. Linux/macOS provider structs can exist now but must return Missing until they can prove real OS state.
  • Audit should record proof summaries/provenance, not raw firewall rules or secrets.

Linux/macOS shape:

  • Linux containment provider verifies owned namespace/cgroup/seccomp-style isolation handle, returns LinuxNamespace + Strong only with evidence.
  • macOS provider returns MacosVmBeta + Beta only for a provider-owned VM/network boundary.
  • Vault-only egress provider verifies a default-deny ruleset allowing only the normalized configured Vault authority/IP:port; public-registry probes are checks over the ruleset, not public network calls.

  1. CLI --containment-available --egress-enforced still yields OperatorAsserted and launch stays blocked.
  2. Public Verified proofs cannot be minted outside provider/test support.
  3. Verified egress for the wrong Vault host blocks before runtime materialization.

  8. A fake package-manager binary is never spawned on blocked or planned high-risk install paths.
  9. Audit/CLI output includes provider id, mechanism, proof status, and reason codes, with no secrets or raw credentials.

Subagent Response: Dewey #subagent-34-response Jun 24, 11:52:20 PM EDT

Returned via close_agent.

Read-only review done. No files edited.

Findings

  • Verified is currently forgeable by any production crate because ContainmentProof and EgressProof fields are public, and launch trusts request-supplied proofs. See whoathere-sandbox/src/lib.rs and whoathere-launch/src/lib.rs. A provider SPI must not let providers directly mint trusted proof structs; providers should return evidence, and one central verifier should mint proofs.
  • EgressProof::permits_only_configured_vault only checks status == Verified and reason_code, not check coverage. With public fields, mandatory negative checks can be bypassed. See whoathere-sandbox/src/lib.rs.
  • Fake/test providers must never be selectable via CLI/config/env or production feature flags. Current CLI assertion flags correctly remain OperatorAsserted (whoathere-cli/src/lib.rs); preserve that boundary.
  • Egress proof must be bound to the exact normalized Vault origin, generated launch context, provider rule generation, and TTL. The current gate only checks host match plus proof status (whoathere-launch/src/lib.rs), so stale/cross-origin/cross-context replay is the main evasion risk.
  • String-host egress checks are too weak for production trust. Provider evidence must prove deny-by-default network enforcement over host/IP/port/protocol/DNS, including public registries, metadata IPs, localhost, IPv6 loopback, and non-Vault loopback ports.

Must Prohibit

  • Fake/fixture/recorded providers in normal builds or production dependency paths.
  • User/workspace-controlled provider loading, provider paths, proof files, or replayed serialized proofs.
  • Any fake provider using the same provider ID, trust domain, or reason codes as a real provider.
  • Upgrading OperatorAsserted into Verified.
  • Runtime materialization or process spawning when provider trust is fake, unknown, stale, incomplete, or mismatched.

Audit / Provenance Fields Add per-proof fields: proof_id, schema version, proof kind, status, trust domain, provider ID/name/version, provider binary/source digest, verified-at/expires-at, request correlation ID, execution mode, command kind/risk, normalized Vault origin/host, sanitized context hash, workspace/source scan hash, enforcement rule/policy hash and generation, host OS/kernel/backend details, raw check summaries, and provider failure reason. For fakes, always emit trust_domain=test_fake.

Acceptance Tests

  • Compile-fail test: external crates cannot construct ProofStatus::Verified proofs by struct literal.
  • Production build test: fake provider symbols/features are absent from normal cargo build.
  • CLI test: assertion flags still block with OperatorAsserted, runtime_materialized=false.
  • Fake-provider test: fake proof is audited but rejected before runtime materialization.
  • Malformed-proof tests: Verified with missing checks, wrong reason, wrong backend, stale TTL, or unknown provider blocks.
  • Replay tests: proof for Vault A fails for Vault B, localhost, IPv6, or changed context hash.
  • Egress tests: public registry, GitHub, metadata IP, non-Vault loopback, IPv6 loopback all denied in proof evidence.
  • Execution test: even with accepted verified proofs, install execution remains disabled and no package manager is spawned.

Subagent Response: Sartre #subagent-47-response Jun 25, 10:06:51 AM EDT

Returned via wait_agent.

Scope note: I could not inspect an actual uncommitted diff because no .git metadata is present under ~/src/whoathere or ~/src/whoathere/whoathere. Findings are from the current source state.

Findings

  • [P1] Malformed or escaped manifests can pass as clean. whoathere-detector/src/lib.rs delegates to substring scanners, and only empty contents or empty job_id fail closed. scan_npm_package_json and scan_pyproject_toml do not parse JSON/TOML, so non-empty invalid metadata, or valid JSON with escaped lifecycle keys, can produce JobState::Passed.
  • [P1] The local admission simulation still promotes synthetic dynamic evidence. whoathere-vault-dev/src/lib.rs marks all selected mandatory jobs as Passed; for complete=true, the profile includes LifecycleDetonation and ImportSmoke from whoathere-evidence/src/lib.rs. Admission then promotes at whoathere-admission/src/lib.rs. If this slice must be metadata-only, this route is outside the boundary even though it does not actually execute detonation/imports.
  • [P2] NPM lifecycle coverage is incomplete. whoathere-detector/src/lib.rs checks only preinstall, install, postinstall, and prepare. Other install-time lifecycle names such as prepublish, preprepare, and postprepare are not flagged, so those manifests can pass the static job.
  • [P2] Static job identity validation is too weak for a public producer API. StaticManifestJobRequest carries profile_id, artifact_digest, and cache_object_key, but run_static_manifest_job only checks job_id. Invalid or mismatched identity fields can still return JobState::Passed; the vault binding path catches some of this later, but the detector API itself is fail-open if reused directly.
  • [P2] The static-manifest dev route defaults unsupported selectors to a passing clean NPM fixture. whoathere-vault-dev/src/lib.rs uses request.contains(...) over the whole raw request, and line 631 falls back to clean metadata. manifest=unknown, missing body, or matching text in headers should fail closed instead of silently passing.
  • [P3] Hash coverage is thin for a security boundary primitive. whoathere-hash/src/lib.rs tests only abc. Add empty input and 55/56/64-byte padding boundary vectors, since this digest is used for log/audit identifiers.

Subagent Response: Jason #subagent-48-response Jun 25, 10:16:51 AM EDT

Returned via wait_agent.

Findings

  • [P1] whoathere-vault-dev/src/lib.rs: the static-manifest route creates a fresh InMemoryJobLogStore per request. The route always uses static-manifest-dev-job-1, so two HTTP calls can store different summaries/digests for the same job ID with no JobIdConflict. This means route-level storage is not append-only across the in-memory dev server lifetime, and duplicate job IDs can effectively be rewritten.
  • [P1] whoathere-job-log/src/lib.rs: the store validates only schema prefix, raw_log_captured, and sha256(summary) == log_digest. It does not parse/cross-check summary fields against SanitizedJobLogEntry fields such as job_id, profile_id, artifact_digest, cache_object_key, or job_kind. A caller can store a correctly hashed summary describing one job under another job ID.
  • [P2] whoathere-detector/src/lib.rs: the sanitized summary is line-oriented but interpolates request metadata without rejecting control characters/newlines. Combined with weak store validation in whoathere-job-log/src/lib.rs, a crafted job_id or profile_id can inject extra summary lines while still hashing cleanly.
  • [P2] whoathere-detector/src/lib.rs: StaticManifestJobOutput has no structured raw_log_captured field. The route supplies that flag from request input at whoathere-vault-dev/src/lib.rs, so the “no raw log capture” invariant is not carried as typed detector output.

Test Gaps

  • No test covers repeated static-manifest route calls with the same job ID but different manifests/digests.
  • No job-log test attempts entry/summary identity mismatches.
  • No detector/store test rejects newline or control-character injection in metadata fields.
  • No detector test asserts output.log_digest == sha256(output.sanitized_log_summary) directly.

Subagent Response: Mencius #subagent-49-response Jun 25, 10:56:41 AM EDT

Returned via wait_agent.

Findings

build_launch_plan creates a challenge subject from the context hash, but launch gating only checks that containment and egress proofs share some bound subject, not that they match proof_challenge.subject: launch/lib.rs:140, launch/lib.rs:196, launch/lib.rs:635. Tests currently accept "launch-unit-test-subject" while the challenge subject is launch-fnv64-...: launch/lib.rs:890. Remediate: require both proofs’ subjects to equal plan.proof_challenge.subject, or gate on a ProviderChallengeAttempt::challenge_satisfied. Add a negative test where both proofs share the same arbitrary subject but not the challenge subject.

  1. P1: Launch does not enforce the generated challenge subject.

LaunchRequest defaults proof_validation_time_unix_seconds to 1, and freshness checks use that request field rather than trusted current time: launch/lib.rs:41, launch/lib.rs:211. Proof provenance has no challenge_id, and test trusted proofs expire at u64::MAX: sandbox/lib.rs:236, sandbox/lib.rs:250. Remediate: compute validation time inside launch from SystemTime, enforce short max TTL/skew, bind proofs to a random challenge nonce/id, and reject reused challenge ids. Add tests proving stale proofs cannot pass by choosing an old validation time.

  1. P1: Replay protection is weak because freshness uses caller-supplied time and proofs are not bound to a challenge nonce/id.

Both challenge ids and launch context hashes use FNV64: sandbox/lib.rs:268, sandbox/lib.rs:593, launch/lib.rs:467. Since proof acceptance compares provenance.context_hash to this value, collision attacks would undermine context binding: launch/lib.rs:641. Remediate: use SHA-256/BLAKE3 or an HMAC over canonical structured data with domain separation.

  1. P1: Context/challenge binding relies on non-cryptographic FNV-1a 64-bit hashes.

ProviderChallengeAttempt flags provider id mismatch, but launch gating never checks provider id, platform, mechanism, or rule_generation_id: sandbox/lib.rs:690, launch/lib.rs:179. rule_generation_id is recorded but not enforced: sandbox/lib.rs:145. Remediate: require a shared verifier session/rule generation, or replace separate proofs with one combined provider attestation. Add tests for mismatched provider/rule generation.

  1. P2: Containment and egress proofs are not atomically bound to the same verifier/rule generation.

Verified egress requires the configured vault plus a fixed mandatory list, but finite probes cannot prove all other egress is denied: sandbox/lib.rs:102, sandbox/lib.rs:492, sandbox/lib.rs:524. The list misses obvious classes like IPv6 localhost and arbitrary RFC1918/link-local endpoints beyond one metadata IP. Remediate: require attested default-deny rule installation plus probe evidence; keep probes as diagnostics, not the basis for the word “only.”

  1. P2: “Only configured vault” can be overclaimed from finite probes.

evaluate_challenge calls prove_containment(mode) with no subject/context/challenge id, while egress gets only subject/vault/probes: sandbox/lib.rs:929, sandbox/lib.rs:941. Remediate: make providers implement prove_challenge(&ProviderVerificationChallenge, mode) returning both proofs, or pass the full challenge to both proof methods.

  1. P2: The provider challenge API does not pass the challenge into containment proof creation.

High-risk installs with all gates present become Planned but still have execution_allowed=false and install_execution_not_enabled: launch/lib.rs:247. launch plan reports allow exit code for any non-blocked plan: cli/lib.rs:1116. Remediate: if --execute is requested and execution_allowed=false, return a nonzero execution exit code or split plan_exit_code from execution_exit_code.

  1. P3: CLI exit status can become misleading once verified proofs are wired.

No edits made.

Completed the Docker Active Probe Executor Harness slice. New command:

whoathere evidence linux-active-probe-docker --subject <id> --context-hash <hash> --vault-host <host> [--image <image>] [--execute] [--json]
